title: Sarvo vai rudraḥ: all this is Rudra
theme: Three statements that everything — the person, being and light, the whole manifold world past and present — is Rudra, each closed with homage.

words.context: Sāyaṇa: Rudra is all because he has entered every body as its living self, «स एव सर्वो जीवरूपेण सर्वशरीरेषु प्रविष्टत्वात्»
Sāyaṇa: the conscious person, apart from inert nature, «प्रकृतिपुरुषयोर्मध्ये जडात्मिकां प्रकृतिमपोह्य चिदात्मकः पुरुषो यो विद्यते»
Sāyaṇa: «अबाधितं सद्रूपं तेजः» — a light whose nature is being, never contradicted

words.role: first of the subjects of the clause

words.meaning: what has come to be — living beings
words.context: Sāyaṇa: «यच्च भूतं चेतनं प्राणिजातमस्ति» — the conscious, the host of living beings
Sāyaṇa: «चेतनाचेतनरूपेण विचित्रं» — manifold as conscious and unconscious

sandhi.rule: -aḥ becomes -o before a voiced sound: sarvo vai; the visarga becomes s before t (P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः)): rudras tasmai.

sandhi.type: visarga before s; t before a nasal
sandhi.rule: The recitation text writes the visarga before s as a doubled s (rudras san); the t of sat becomes n before the nasal m (P. 8.4.45 (यरोऽनुनासिकेऽनुनासिको वा)): san mahaḥ.

sandhi.type: i before a vowel; eṣaḥ before a consonant
sandhi.rule: hi + eṣaḥ → hy eṣaḥ (P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि)); the visarga of eṣaḥ is dropped before a consonant (P. 6.1.132 (एतत्तदोः सुलोपोऽकोरनञ्समासे हलि)): eṣa rudraḥ.

sandhi_exceptions.note: namo · astu: the o of namo is kept before a and the a is not elided (classical namo ’stu); Vedic recitation keeps e and o before a inside a pāda (P. 6.1.115 (प्रकृत्याऽन्तःपादमव्यपरे)). All witnesses print namo astu.
namo · astu again, in the refrain that closes the anuvāka; the same Vedic keeping of o before a.

morphology.note: Sāyaṇa reads sat and mahaḥ together as ‘light that is being’, and supports sat with the Chāndogya’s «सदेव सोम्येदमग्र आसीत्» (ChU 6.2.1). Sat could also be read as the participle ‘being [Rudra], [he is] light’; the commentators take it as a noun.
The relative clause viśvaṃ bhūtaṃ … jāyamānaṃ ca yat (‘whatever is …’) has no main clause of its own; the next line, sarvo hy eṣa rudraḥ, completes it: whatever is, all that is Rudra.

translation.literal: All, truly, [is] Rudra; to him, to Rudra, let there be homage. The person, truly, [is] Rudra, being, light; homage, homage. The universe, what has come to be, the world, manifold, born in many ways and being born — whatever [is]: all this, indeed, [is] Rudra; to him, to Rudra, let there be homage.
translation.readable: Rudra is all that is: homage to Rudra. Rudra is the Person, being and light: homage, homage. Whatever there is — the world, all that has come to be, manifold, born in many forms and still being born — all of it is Rudra. Homage to Rudra.

syntax: Three short identifications (sarvo vai rudraḥ; puruṣo vai rudraḥ, san mahaḥ), each followed by homage in the dative (tasmai rudrāya namo astu; namo namaḥ). The third line is a long relative clause with no verb, gathering the world in all its tenses; the refrain sarvo hy eṣa rudraḥ, with hi giving the ground, completes it and repeats the homage.

ambiguities.note: ‘All’ as the whole of things, or Rudra present in every body as its living self — Sāyaṇa’s and the anonymous commentator’s reading. The text says only that all is Rudra.
Read by the commentators as ‘light that is being’ (sat and mahas as nouns). It could also be heard as ‘being [Rudra], he is light’. The commentators do not discuss the alternative.

metre.name: mixed
metre.note: Not a regular metre: the checker counts 14, 13, 20 and 15 syllables in the four lines. The first, second and fourth lines are short formulas of homage; the third, the list of all that is born, runs to 20 syllables.

beginner: This passage makes one large claim three times. First: Rudra is all. Then: Rudra is the Person, being itself, and light. Finally, after listing everything there is — the world, every living thing, all that has been born and all that is being born now — it says that all of this is Rudra. After each statement it bows: homage to Rudra. The old commentators explain the claim this way: Rudra has entered every living body as its inner life, and the conscious Person that appears as Rudra is the light of being itself. The passage praises; it does not argue, and it does not say what reciting it brings. Its repeated ending, ‘homage to Rudra’, is what makes the list of everything into an act of reverence.
analogy: Like a refrain in a song: each verse names something new, and the refrain brings every verse back to the same point.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: That all is Rudra; that the person is Rudra, being and light; and that whatever there is, the world born and being born, is Rudra. Each statement ends in homage to him.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa and the anonymous commentator explain that Rudra, the husband of Pārvatī known from the Purāṇas, has entered every body as its living self: «यो रुद्रः पार्वतीपतिः पुराणेषु प्रसिद्धः स एव सर्वो जीवरूपेण सर्वशरीरेषु प्रविष्टत्वात्». The person of the second line is the conscious principle as distinct from inert nature, which takes Rudra’s form for the sake of devotees: «स एव भक्तानुग्रहाय रुद्रमूर्तिरूपेणावभासते».

commentary.q: Why can the world be called Rudra?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Because, Sāyaṇa says, the world cannot be described as real apart from him: «तव्द्यतिरेकेण वास्तवस्य जगतो निरूपयितुमशक्यत्वात्». Being and light he explains through the Chāndogya: «सदेव सोम्येदमग्र आसीत्».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa treats this anuvāka (his 16), kad rudrāya (10.25, his 17) and namo hiraṇyabāhave (10.22, his 18) as a group, and says their mantras are known in the manuals as the Tvaritarudra: «अनेनानुवाकत्रयेणोक्तानां मन्त्राणां त्वरितरुद्राख्या मन्त्रकल्पेषु प्रसिद्धा».

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this anuvāka is in the edition’s sources (Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not available here; Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara’s comment on it is empty in the copy used). The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa agree word for word.

parallels.note: The Chāndogya’s ‘all this is Brahman’ makes the same kind of claim of identity that this anuvāka makes of Rudra.

contemporary.text: The passage refuses to leave anything out: the inert and the living, what has already come to be and what is coming to be now. Whatever one makes of its theology, the habit it models — taking in the whole before bowing — is a discipline of attention that works against seeing only the part one prefers. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: The passage says ‘all is Rudra’ three times, in different words. What does the repetition add?
reflect.deeper: Sāyaṇa says the world cannot be described as real apart from Rudra. How is that claim different from saying the world was made by him?
reflect.practice: Look at one ordinary object near you and think of everything it took for it to come into being.

references.text: Sāyaṇa comments on this anuvāka as his anuvāka 16 (the concordance maps it correctly); the anonymous commentator’s text repeats his almost word for word.
Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara’s anuvāka 16, which corresponds to this one, is empty («…») in the copy used; the edition’s concordance maps nothing here.

flags.note: Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara’s comment on this anuvāka is missing from the copy used, so his reading could not be compared.
